name: Kentucky
summary_text: Trans visitors to Kentucky stand under the United States federal framework on travel documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and bars self-selection of gender on passports and visas; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents. Visa discretion, including the February 2025 refusal pathway for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events, and checkpoint screening procedures apply on arrival in Louisville, Lexington and elsewhere in Kentucky as they do in every other state.  Kentucky's own instrument is Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 when the Kentucky General Assembly voted to override Governor Andy Beshear's veto. The statute does two things relevant here: it restricts which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools, and it bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors in the commonwealth. It is the single 2023 statute carrying the school facility restriction.  Implementation runs through local school districts. In April 2023 the Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance to districts on applying the 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to tread cautiously with the bathroom provisions. The department does not enforce the restriction directly; districts do.  The care prohibition took effect on 14 July 2023, when United States District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month. The order allows Kentucky to bar transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the statute, and the ACLU of Kentucky called the ruling a temporary setback.  The Movement Advancement Project's equality map catalogues Kentucky's 2023 K-12 facility ban among its state-by-state entries on bans against transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, placing the commonwealth within a national pattern rather than an isolated rule.

sources.title: Executive Order banning conversion therapy on minors - Gov. Beshear Sept 18, 2024 + city ordinances
sources.documents: Statewide ban on conversion therapy on minors; prior local bans showing patchwork rights machinery.
sources.detail: Illegal since September 18, 2024 when Governor Beshear signed executive order; Covington March 2020 by 5-0, Louisville Sept 2020 by 24-1, Lexington May 2021 unanimous by Lexington-Fayette Urban County Council

name: Louisiana
summary_text: Louisiana stands under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992, and the American Civil Liberties Union's suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs remains in federal court. By March 2025 trans and nonbinary travellers reported passports being confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad. Entry screening carries separate exposure. Since 25 February 2025 the State Department has flagged visa applicants with an internal marking, treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth, in the context of barring trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports. Separately, Transportation Security Administration checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller. Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state in the country: 24.7 per 100,000 people per year reported, on 19 recorded victims, against 23.5 for the state ranked safest. The count rests on a base of 428 victims recorded across the United States between 2008 and 2025, and every figure in that base is an undercount floor. A national analysis drawing on that data cautions that rankings built on legal risk do not sort physical safety: the states holding the worst law carry the highest rate. Violence in Louisiana has also produced prosecutions of the people attacked. In August 2026 a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who suffered a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested, and the Sheriff's Office reported no other arrests that day. Rush was denied hospital care, jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence. The plea deal offered to the victims was not signed. The same municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances, placing local restroom access for trans residents and visitors on a restrictive footing at the time of the attack. Custody is a documented site of harm. On 2 April 2024 Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates. She was at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person killed that year and the fifth in April alone, and such deaths are systematically under- or mis-reported.

sources.title: Obergefell v. Hodges, U.S. Supreme Court
sources.documents: Invalidated Louisiana same-sex marriage bans (1988/1999 Civil Code provisions and 2004 constitutional bans on marriage and civil unions); requires state to license same-sex marriages since June 26, 2015; Governor Bobby Jindal said state would comply two days later.
sources.detail: Citation visible: U.S. Supreme Court ruling June 26, 2015

sources.title: Adar v. Smith / Pavan v. Smith
sources.documents: Documents birth-certificate machinery for same-sex parents: Louisiana successfully defended refusal to amend certificate for Louisiana-born child adopted in New York by married same-sex couple; Supreme Court rejected Lambda Legal review Oct 11, 2011; Obergefell and Pavan v. sources.detail: Citation visible: U.S. Supreme Court denial Oct 11, 2011, Lambda Legal representing plaintiffs; Pavan v. Smith June 2017

sources.title: Louisiana hate crime statute (1997) and Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act
sources.documents: State penalty-enhancement law covers crimes motivated by victim sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation, first in Deep South after 5-year lobbying; does not include gender identity, which must be prosecuted federally under 2009 federal Act signed by President Barack Obama.
